pos: n. (a delay of the execution of a sentence of death)
etymology: Origin uncertain. Webster: to respite after sentence of death; to suspend or delay the execution for a time. Also a respite, an interval of ease.
biblical_def:
I will add unto thy days fifteen years; and I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria. The LORD said the same to Hezekiah through Isaiah: I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen years.

A reprieve is not a pardon. The sentence stands. The day of execution is moved. Hezekiah had been told to set his house in order, for he would die. The added fifteen years were a delay granted to a praying man, not a repeal of death. Webster's first sense is exactly that: the criminal is not cleared. He is respited.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to respite after sentence of death; to suspend or delay the execution for a time. As a noun, the temporary suspension of the execution of a sentence of death.
webster_full: REPRIEVE, v.t. To respite after sentence of death; to suspend or delay the execution of for a time.
To grant a respite to; to relieve for a time from any suffering.
REPRIEVE, n. The temporary suspension of the execution of sentence of death on a criminal.
scriptures: And I will add unto thy days fifteen years; and I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria; and I will defend this city for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake.
Isa 38:5
Go, and say to Hezekiah, Thus saith the LORD, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen years.
corruption_summary: The age treats a delay of judgment as if the judgment had been cancelled.
corruption_paragraphs: Hezekiah's added years did not make him immortal. They moved the day. A reprieve that is preached as a pardon trains men to despise the sentence that still stands.
Webster keeps the word on the sentenced man. The execution is suspended. It is not undone. Conscience, he notes, is not secured by company that only reprieves a man from melancholy.
roots_summary: No biblical headword. The field is a delayed death, as in Hezekiah's added fifteen years (2Ki 20:6; Isa 38:5).
roots_lines: Fifteen years is a measured delay. The LORD names the number. He does not say the man will not die.
A reprieve is mercy in time. It is not the blotting out of the record.
usage: I will add unto thy days fifteen years — a reprieve with a date on it.
I have seen thy tears — the delay was an answer to prayer, not a right.

pos: n. (an act of oblivion; a general pardon of offenses against the government)
etymology: Greek, from a negative and memory: a not-remembering. Webster: an act of oblivion; a general pardon of the offenses of subjects against the government, or the proclamation of such pardon.
biblical_def:
I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins. I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

Amnesty, in the civil sense, is a general pardon proclaimed by a government. Scripture's greater act is not a statute. It is the LORD blotting out transgressions for His own sake, and promising not to remember them. A civil amnesty can quiet a rebellion. It cannot cast sin into the sea. Only God does that.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an act of oblivion; a general pardon of the offenses of subjects against the government, or the proclamation of such pardon.
webster_full: AMNESTY, n. An act of oblivion; a general pardon of the offenses of subjects against the government, or the proclamation of such pardon.
scriptures: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.

And they shall teach no more every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the LORD: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the LORD: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.
Mic 7:19
He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
corruption_summary: The age treats a political forgetting as if it were the forgiveness of God.
corruption_paragraphs: A proclamation can stop a prosecution. It cannot blot out transgressions for the LORD's own sake. Isaiah 43:25 names the Actor. It is not the senate.
Jeremiah 31:34 ties the not-remembering to the new covenant, and to men knowing the LORD. An amnesty that leaves men strangers to God is only a civil quiet.
roots_summary: Greek, a not-remembering. The biblical counterpart is the LORD who will not remember sins (Isa 43:25; Jer 31:34).
roots_lines: Oblivion is Webster's first noun. Scripture's oblivion is God's, and it is mercy, not a lapse.
Micah 7:19 puts the sins in the depths of the sea. That is farther than a proclamation can reach.
usage: I will not remember thy sins — amnesty that only God can proclaim.
Cast all their sins into the depths of the sea — forgetting that is an act, not a mood.

pos: n. (a person excluded from the benefit and protection of the law)
etymology: English, out and law. Webster: a person excluded from the benefit of the law, or deprived of its protection. To outlaw is to deprive of that benefit; to proscribe.
biblical_def:
If they be the children of men, cursed be they before the LORD; for they have driven me out this day from abiding in the inheritance of the LORD, saying, Go, serve other gods. The LORD loveth judgment, and forsaketh not his saints; they are preserved for ever: but the seed of the wicked shall be cut off.

An outlaw is a man put outside the protection of the law. David, hunted by Saul, describes the sentence his enemies would put on him: driven from the inheritance, told to go serve other gods. That is proscription. Scripture does not give every private man the right Webster says old law once gave, to kill the outlaw. The LORD forsaketh not his saints. A man driven from the inheritance is not thereby abandoned by God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a person excluded from the benefit of the law, or deprived of its protection. To outlaw is to deprive of the benefit and protection of law; to proscribe.
webster_full: OUTLAW, n. A person excluded from the benefit of the law, or deprived of its protection.
Formerly any person might kill an outlaw; but it is now held unlawful for any person to put to death an outlaw except the sheriff, who has a warrant for that purpose.
OUTLAW, v.t. To deprive of the benefit and protection of law; to proscribe.
scriptures: Now therefore, I pray thee, let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If the LORD have stirred thee up against me, let him accept an offering: but if they be the children of men, cursed be they before the LORD; for they have driven me out this day from abiding in the inheritance of the LORD, saying, Go, serve other gods.
For the LORD loveth judgment, and forsaketh not his saints; they are preserved for ever: but the seed of the wicked shall be cut off.
corruption_summary: The age romanticizes the outlaw, as if exclusion from the law's protection were a kind of freedom.
corruption_paragraphs: David does not boast of being driven out. He calls the driving a curse, and he asks the king to hear him. Proscription is a wound, not a costume.
Psalm 37:28 keeps the saint inside the LORD's preservation even when men have put him outside the inheritance. The outlaw of a court is not therefore the outlaw of God.
roots_summary: English compound. The biblical picture is a man driven from the inheritance of the LORD (1Sa 26:19).
roots_lines: Out of the law means out of its benefit, not above it. Webster's old license to kill the outlaw is itself now unlawful except by warrant.
David's complaint names the spiritual aim of the proscription: Go, serve other gods. Exclusion from the inheritance was meant to exile him from worship.
usage: They have driven me out this day from abiding in the inheritance — David's name for proscription.
The LORD forsaketh not his saints — the sentence that outlasts the outlawry.

pos: n. (an insurrection of soldiers or seamen against the authority of their commanders)
etymology: Latin muto, to change. Webster: an insurrection of soldiers or seamen against the authority of their commanders; open resistance of officers. He notes that older authors used the word of civil sedition, but that in his day it belonged to army and navy.
biblical_def:
All the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron: Would God that we had died in the land of Egypt. And they said one to another, Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt. On the morrow the congregation murmured against Moses and against Aaron, saying, Ye have killed the people of the LORD. Certain of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul.

Mutiny is the camp rising against the commander God appointed. Israel did not merely complain of the menu. They proposed another captain and a return to Egypt. The band against Paul is the same shape in a city: men under a curse, set to kill the man who carried the authority of the gospel. Webster confines the statute word to soldiers and seamen. Scripture judges the act wherever men refuse the officer God has set over them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an insurrection of soldiers or seamen against the authority of their commanders; open resistance of officers or opposition to their authority.
webster_full: MUTINY, n. An insurrection of soldiers or seamen against the authority of their commanders; open resistance of officers or opposition to their authority.
A mutiny is properly the act of numbers. Any attempt to excite opposition to lawful authority is declared mutiny by the British mutiny act.
Webster notes that older authors applied the word to civil sedition, but that in his day it belonged to soldiers and seamen.
scriptures: Num 14:2

And all the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron: and the whole congregation said unto them, Would God that we had died in the land of Egypt! or would God we had died in this wilderness!
Num 14:4
And they said one to another, Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt.
But on the morrow all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron, saying, Ye have killed the people of the LORD.
And when it was day, certain of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul.
corruption_summary: The age calls mutiny conscience, so that refusing a lawful commander is praised as authenticity.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 14:4 is the proposal under the murmur: let us make a captain. The new captain is the point of the mutiny. Complaint that seeks another head has already left the post.
Acts 23:12 shows a band under a curse. The curse does not sanctify the plot. It aggravates it. They bound themselves to kill the apostle.
roots_summary: Latin muto, to change. The biblical exhibits are the camp against Moses (Num 14) and the band against Paul (Act 23:12).
roots_lines: To change the commander is the root Webster gives. Israel said, let us make a captain.
The murmur of the morrow, after judgment had already fallen, is mutiny that will not learn.
usage: Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt — mutiny with a destination.
They bound themselves under a curse — a band set to kill the commander of the gospel.

pos: v. (to steal a human being and carry him into another country or state)
etymology: English, originally the stealing of a child. Webster widens it: to steal a human being, man, woman, or child; or to seize and forcibly carry any person from his own country or state into another.
biblical_def:
He that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death. If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him; then that thief shall die; and thou shalt put evil away from among you.

To kidnap is to steal a person. Scripture does not treat that theft as a property dispute. The penalty is death. The man found in the hand of the thief, not yet sold, is already enough. Making merchandise of a brother is the aggravation Deuteronomy names. The evil is to be put away from among the people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to steal a human being, man, woman, or child; or to seize and forcibly carry away any person from his own country or state into another.
webster_full: KIDNAP, v.t. To steal a human being, man, woman or child; or to seize and forcibly carry away any person whatever from his own country or state into another.
scriptures: And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
Deu 24:7
If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him; then that thief shall die; and thou shalt put evil away from among you.
corruption_summary: The age treats the theft of a person as a lesser crime than the theft of goods, when Scripture makes it a capital evil.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 21:16 does not wait for the sale. Found in his hand is enough for death. The carrying is the crime.
Deuteronomy 24:7 names merchandise. A brother turned into goods is the definition of the sin. The statute that shrugs at that theft has left the law of Moses.
roots_summary: No polite biblical synonym. The charge is man-stealing (Exo 21:16; Deu 24:7), punished by death.
roots_lines: Stealeth a man is the commandment's own verb. Kidnap is that verb in later English.
Put evil away from among you is the congregational sentence. The thief is not managed. He is removed.
usage: He that stealeth a man, and selleth him — the capital statute.
Maketh merchandise of him — a brother priced and carried off.

pos: n. (a judicial setting free from the charge of an offense)
etymology: From acquit, to set free. Webster: a judicial setting free, or deliverance from the charge of an offense, as by verdict of a jury or sentence of a court.
biblical_def:
If there be a controversy between men, and they come unto judgment, then they shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked. He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD. Pilate said of Jesus, I, having examined him before you, have found no fault in this man touching those things whereof ye accuse him.

An acquittal is a court declaring that the charge does not stand. When the man is righteous, that declaration is the judge's duty. When the man is wicked, the same declaration is an abomination. Pilate found no fault and did not acquit. The word is not a feeling of innocence. It is a judgment spoken.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a judicial setting free, or deliverance from the charge of an offense, as by verdict of a jury or sentence of a court.
webster_full: ACQUITTAL, n. A judicial setting free, or deliverance from the charge of an offense; as, by verdict of a jury, or sentence of a court.
The acquittal of a principal operates as an acquittal of the accessories.
scriptures: Deu 25:1
If there be a controversy between men, and they come unto judgment, that the judges may judge them; then they shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked.
He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.

Said unto them, Ye have brought this man unto me, as one that perverteth the people: and, behold, I, having examined him before you, have found no fault in this man touching those things whereof ye accuse him:
corruption_summary: The age treats acquittal as proof of innocence, and also as a prize to be won for the guilty.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 25:1 binds the judge both ways. Justify the righteous. Condemn the wicked. An acquittal that ignores that pair is not justice. Proverbs 17:15 calls it abomination.
Pilate's finding of no fault, followed by a handing over, is the warning. A true word that is not carried into the sentence is not an acquittal. It is a cowardice wearing the language of examination.
roots_summary: The biblical duty is to justify the righteous and condemn the wicked (Deu 25:1). Acquittal is the first half, spoken in court.
roots_lines: Justify, in that verse, is the judge's word for the man who is in the right. It is not a private opinion.
Proverbs 17:15 pairs the false acquittal with the false condemnation. Both are abomination.
usage: They shall justify the righteous — the acquittal the judge owes.
I have found no fault in this man — a finding that Pilate would not finish.

pos: n. (the answer of a jury to the court; a true declaration)
etymology: Latin verum dictum, a true declaration. Webster: the answer of a jury given to the court concerning the matter of fact committed to them. Also a decision or judgment pronounced.
biblical_def:
They shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked. He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD. Judas, when he saw that he was condemned, brought again the thirty pieces of silver.

A verdict is a declaration that claims to be true. The Latin name says so. Scripture requires the declaration to match the man: righteous justified, wicked condemned. A verdict that swaps those two is not a close call. It is an abomination. Judas heard a condemnation and knew what he had purchased. The silver came back. The verdict of the council stood, and the Innocent died under it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the answer of a jury given to the court concerning any matter of fact committed to their trial. From Latin verum dictum, a true declaration.
webster_full: VERDICT, n. The answer of a jury given to the court concerning any matter of fact in any cause, civil or criminal, committed to their trial and examination.
scriptures: Deu 25:1
If there be a controversy between men, and they come unto judgment, that the judges may judge them; then they shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked.
He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.
Mat 27:3
Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,
corruption_summary: The age treats a verdict as the voice of the crowd, so that a true declaration is whatever the louder side pronounces.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's verum dictum is a true declaration, not a popular one. A jury can answer and still lie. Proverbs 17:15 does not excuse the lie because it wore a robe.
Matthew 27:3 is the verdict that condemned the Just. Judas saw it and brought the money back. The council kept the verdict. The silver in the temple did not revise it.
roots_summary: Latin verum dictum, a true saying. The biblical test is Deuteronomy 25:1: justify the righteous, condemn the wicked.
roots_lines: True declaration is the name. A false verdict keeps the form and loses the Latin.
Matthew 27:3 shows a condemnation that the betrayer himself could not live with, and that the court would not undo.
usage: Justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked — the only verdict that is not an abomination.
When he saw that he was condemned — Judas looking at a verdict he had helped buy.

pos: n. (a written accusation of a crime, preferred under oath to a court)
etymology: From indict, to charge in writing. Webster: a written accusation or formal charge of a crime or misdemeanor, preferred by a grand jury under oath to a court. Also the paper containing that accusation.
biblical_def:
The Jews which came down from Jerusalem stood round about, and laid many and grievous complaints against Paul, which they could not prove. Tertullus began to accuse him. Pilate said, Ye have brought this man unto me, as one that perverteth the people. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.

An indictment is an accusation put in writing and brought into court. Scripture knows the grievous complaint that cannot be proved, and the smooth accuser who begins with flattery. The writing does not make the charge true. The ninth commandment still governs the hand that drafts it. A charge that cannot be proved is not a lesser indictment. It is a false witness with a seal.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a written accusation or formal charge of a crime or misdemeanor, preferred by a grand jury under oath to a court. Also the paper containing the accusation.
webster_full: INDICTMENT, n. A written accusation or formal charge of a crime or misdemeanor, preferred by a grand jury under oath to a court.
The paper or parchment containing the accusation of a grand jury.
scriptures: Act 25:7
And when he was come, the Jews which came down from Jerusalem stood round about, and laid many and grievous complaints against Paul, which they could not prove.
Act 24:2
And when he was called forth, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, Seeing that by thee we enjoy great quietness, and that very worthy deeds are done unto this nation by thy providence,

Said unto them, Ye have brought this man unto me, as one that perverteth the people: and, behold, I, having examined him before you, have found no fault in this man touching those things whereof ye accuse him:
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
corruption_summary: The age treats a written charge as if the writing itself were proof.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 25:7 is the apostolic exhibit. Many and grievous complaints, which they could not prove. The number of charges did not supply the missing proof.
Tertullus opens the accusation with praise of the judge. The flattery is part of the indictment's strategy. A false witness that begins politely is still a false witness.
roots_summary: No single biblical headword. The field is the unproved complaint (Act 25:7) and the false witness (Exo 20:16).
roots_lines: A writing under oath is Webster's form. Scripture requires the thing written to be true.
Luke 23:14 records an accusation examined and found empty. The indictment did not create the fault.
usage: Many and grievous complaints against Paul, which they could not prove — an indictment without a case.
Thou shalt not bear false witness — the commandment on the hand that drafts the charge.
